title: Credit cards grew 12 straight months — longest run in 11 months
body: Credit cards outstanding have grown for 12 consecutive months, extending the streak from 11 periods prior. Streak extended from 11 to 12 periods — the longest run since the 16-period streak that ended in Jun 2025. The current streak began in Jul 2025 and has now surpassed the Dec 2024 level.
implication: The credit card market has locked into its longest growth run in 11 months — the 12-period streak is the strongest since Jun 2025's 16-period run and confirms issuers have re-established sustained expansion momentum after the Oct 2025 purge. The Jun 2025 reset was a one-time event, and the current run confirms the market has entered a new growth phase with no signs of deceleration.

title: Credit cards +9.57% YoY — fastest growth in 17 months
body: Credit cards outstanding grew 9.57% year-on-year in Jun 2026, up 1.10 points from 8.47% prior period. YoY growth re-accelerated for the fifth consecutive period: 7.7% in Feb 2026 → 8.0% in Mar 2026 → 8.1% in Apr 2026 → 8.5% in May 2026 → 9.6% in Jun 2026. The rate is now at the upper end of the 18-period range (6.7%–9.6%).
implication: Credit card growth has fully reversed its deceleration trend and is now accelerating at the fastest pace in 17 months — the 9.57% rate is the strongest since Jan 2025 and confirms the purge-driven slowdown has ended. The five-period re-acceleration (7.7% → 8.0% → 8.1% → 8.5% → 9.6%) is the longest sustained acceleration in the dataset, and the 9.57% rate is only 0.2 points below the Jan 2025 peak (9.4%), signaling the market is on track to return to near-double-digit growth within one period. The recovery is complete, and the market is now accelerating beyond the pre-purge baseline.

title: CC spend YoY — ecommerce 30.6% vs in-store POS 22.1%
body: On a year-on-year basis, credit card ecommerce transaction volume grew 30.6% and in-store POS volume grew 22.1% as of Jun 2026. Year-on-year removes the heavy seasonality in the monthly numbers — online is outpacing in-store on a clean comparison.
implication: Credit card spend is growing across both channels year-on-year (ecom faster). A spend mix tilting online is a mix of more card-not-present volume, where fraud and dispute rates run higher — so the channel mix carries risk information the headline spend growth does not.

Online (CNP) is the faster-growing channel on a year-on-year basis
Channel mix shift changes the fraud and dispute profile — risk models must track mix, not just total spend

title: PSB banks hold 63.8% of debit cards — SFB gaining share in Jun 2026
body: Public sector banks account for 63.8% of total debit cards outstanding in Jun 2026 (-0.2pp vs prior month). Private banks hold 25.9%. SFB banks are the fastest-growing category (+0.1pp share gain).
implication: PSBs (government-owned banks like SBI, PNB, Bank of Baroda) hold 63.8% of debit cards, largely because of Jan Dhan — the government scheme that opened basic bank accounts for millions of low-income households. Many of these accounts have little activity. If you're using debit transaction data for credit assessment, PSB debit data needs to be treated very differently from, say, HDFC or Kotak debit customers.

title: Gap: DC ATM cash at 80.4% of DC volume — digital transition is incomplete
body: Despite growth in digital payments, ATM cash withdrawals still account for 80.4% of total debit card transaction volume in Jun 2026 (-0.2pp vs prior month). DC ecommerce is only 5.2% of DC volume. India's debit card base remains overwhelmingly cash-dependent.
implication: 80.4% of debit card spending is ATM cash. Cash leaves no digital record — you can't tell where it was spent or on what. For lenders trying to assess a debit card holder's financial behaviour, the transaction history is mostly blank. Bureau scores (CIBIL, Experian) remain the primary tool for this segment — debit transaction data alone isn't enough yet.

title: UPI QR 16.9% YoY — stable high-growth phase continues
body: UPI QR codes grew 16.87% year-on-year in Jun 2026, up 0.44 points from 16.43% in May 2026. YoY growth held steady 16.4% → 16.9%, a marginal 0.4-point gain — the rate has stabilised in the 15–17% range across the 18-period series, with Jun's 16.9% near the median.
implication: The 16.9% YoY rate confirms UPI QR deployment is in a stable, high-growth phase — the network is adding 11–12 crore codes annually with no signs of saturation. The rate has held in the 15–17% range for 14 consecutive months, even as the base has risen from 66.24 crore to 79.26 crore codes. UPI QR is the only acceptance infrastructure channel with sustained double-digit growth and structural expansion momentum, while POS is contracting at an unprecedented rate.

title: Gap: Offsite ATMs declining -0.7% MoM — rural cash access contracting
body: Offsite ATMs fell 0.7% MoM in Jun 2026 (now 73,426), while onsite ATMs grew +0.1% MoM. Offsite ATMs serve rural and semi-urban populations where branch presence is limited — their decline reduces physical cash access for underserved geographies.

When these decline and digital payments haven't reached those areas yet, rural borrowers lose their easiest way to access cash for repayment. If you have loans in rural geographies, check whether ATM coverage in those areas is shrinking — it can make EMI collection harder.

title: Gap: Top 5 banks hold 91.4% of POS terminals — acquiring market is highly concentrated
body: In Jun 2026, the top 5 banks account for 91.4% of all deployed POS terminals in India. RBL BANK LTD leads at 26.7% market share. All remaining banks combined share less than 8.6% of merchant acquiring infrastructure.
implication: 91.4% of all POS machines in India are owned by just 5 banks — and so is most of the merchant transaction data that comes with them. If you're building merchant credit products (loans to shopkeepers or small businesses) and don't have data partnerships with these top banks, you're working with an incomplete picture. Alternate sources — GST filings, UPI transaction data — can partially fill this gap.

chain: Top 5 banks own 91.4% of POS terminals — merchant acquiring infrastructure highly concentrated
Merchant transaction data (sales history needed for credit underwriting) controlled by the same 5 institutions
Merchant credit underwriting without data partnerships with these banks requires alternates — GST filings, UPI feeds

title: Credit cards mix rotating toward Small Finance Banks (+0.76 pp share in a year)
body: Compared with the same month a year ago, the biggest share gains in credit cards came from Small Finance Banks +0.76 pp; Private Sector Banks +0.10 pp. The ground came from Foreign Banks -0.58 pp; Public Sector Banks -0.28 pp. In all, 0.86 pp of the mix changed hands.
implication: This is a composition read: it says where the mix is shifting, not why and not what happens next. Watch whether Small Finance Banks holds its gains next month before reading the shift as a trend.

chain: Each segment's share of credit cards is compared with the same month a year earlier — the change is in percentage points of the mix.
Top gainer: Small Finance Banks at +0.76 pp. Biggest cession: Foreign Banks at -0.58 pp.
Rotation mass — the share that changed hands — is 0.86 pp.

title: Debit cards in force grew while debit card spend fell (+3.35 pp apart over a year)
body: Debit cards in force and debit card spend normally move together — they are two readings of the same activity. Over the past year they have come apart. Debit cards in force grew over the year; debit card spend fell. Measured as debit cards in force minus debit card spend, the two year-on-year rates are +3.35 pp apart.
implication: A gap between debit cards in force and debit card spend is a question, not a conclusion: the two sides can part company because behaviour changed, because one side has a base effect, or because reporting shifted. Watch whether the gap closes next month — a pair that stays apart for several months is telling you the relationship itself has changed.

chain: Debit cards in force and debit card spend are a declared pair: each side's growth is measured against the same month a year earlier.
Debit cards in force grew over the year; debit card spend fell.
The gap between the two rates — debit cards in force minus debit card spend — is +3.35 pp, wide enough to count as a divergence rather than ordinary drift.
